items.cleanReaderHtml:
Geoengineers have an ingenious plan to rescue the world’s most famous ice-skating race from global warming

“It giet oan,” Henk Kroes, veteran “ice master,” told a room full of reporters on January 2, 1997: “It is happening.”

Kroes was referring to the Elfstedentocht , a 125-mile ice skating competition in the northern Netherlands province of Friesland. For more than a century, the race has been as much a competition as a national celebration. “Never am I happier,” wrote the 17th-century playwright and skating enthusiast Gerbrand Bredero, “as when I am gliding over ice.” The feeling was passed down over the ages in the Netherlands.

The racecourse circles through 11 picturesque Friesland cities. It takes skaters across lakes, winding rivers, and canals. It begins with 300 speed skaters competing for the trophy, followed by an unruly train of nearly 20,000 leisure skaters in their wake.

Kroes, who at the time served as chairman of the Royal Association of the Friesian Eleven Cities, was expressing a mix of relief and excitement.

Race officials had just reported that the ice was 6 inches thick, just barely meeting the minimum safety requirements for the event to proceed. If the ice was any thinner, it wouldn’t hold the weight of the skaters. For years, race officials had worried that sections of the course wouldn’t freeze at all.

Today in the Netherlands Kroes’ words—spoken in his native Frisian dialect—mostly inspire a nostalgic sadness. Due to global warming, there has not been another official Elfstedentocht since 1997. And climate scientists say it is becoming increasingly unlikely that we will ever see one again.

The biggest natural ice-skating competition in the world, the first Elfstedentocht was held in 1909. It almost immediately became one of the most beloved sporting events in the country, rivaling professional football. Perhaps the most iconic iteration of the race—and one that feels especially far removed from the situation today—was the so-called “Hell of ‘63,” when strong winds and temperatures low enough to freeze eyelids kept nearly 99 percent of the nearly 10,000 participants from reaching the finish line.

Frisians in particular remember not just the bitter cold, but also the warmth of their own community. Throughout the 20th century, ordinary economic activity in the province froze to a halt whenever a race was imminent, while the monotony and drudgery of ordinary life melted away like snow in the sun.

Archeological evidence suggests that people living in the Netherlands have been skating across ice in some capacity since the days of the Roman Empire, whose northern border stopped just short of Friesland’s southern edge. During the late Middle Ages, when Dutch winters grew colder as a result of a regional cooling period sometimes referred to as the Little Ice Age, frozen rivers turned into highways, keeping towns connected as land routes became all but impassable. As documented by painters like Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Hendrick Avercamp, skating also proved a popular pastime, enjoyed by peasants and aristocrats alike.

According to the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute, which issues weather forecasts and studies climate trends, the number of ice days—a 24-hour period where the maximum air temperature remains below 32 degrees F—has been declining ever since the 1960s, from an average of 11 per year to just 3. The average temperature of ice days has also been increasing: Entire days that remained below 14 degrees F, once relatively common, have not occurred since 1987 in the Netherlands.

As winters warm, a skill that was once as common and culturally definitive to the Dutch identity as cycling is set to fade away while the Elfstedentocht transforms from a living tradition into a bittersweet memory of colder, happier days.

Unwilling to accept the climatic erosion of a cultural institution, the Netherlands’ brightest science and engineering minds have sought solutions that could preserve the national pastime with a triptych of ingenious ways to fool Mother Nature and get skaters back on the ice.

But using brute technological force to create conditions cold enough to sustain ice is highly impractical. The Elfstedentocht ’s waters cannot be cooled the way we cool artificial ice rinks. In 2021, Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant reported that the 720 diesel-powered industrial-grade chillers needed to do so—though comparatively cheap at a “sponsorable” €90 million—would pump so much CO 2 into the atmosphere (more than 17,000 tons) that it would be more sustainable to fly all 30,000 preregistered contestants (members of the Royal Association of the Friesian Eleven Cities) with their skates at the ready to a lake in the Austrian Alps.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.

“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”

Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.

Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
set of food with healthyl fats and omega-3, laid out in the shape of a heart. Health concept

Trying to drive down your cholesterol by changing your diet can be frustrating. You swap out regular bacon for turkey bacon, eat more oatmeal, and at the end of the day it might not even make a dent in your LDL levels. And yet, dietary interventions seem to work wonders for some people. While it’s tempting to chalk up stubborn cholesterol numbers to genetics, a new study published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology is complicating the picture.

“We have people who come into the clinic and say, ‘I changed my diet, and it made no difference in my cholesterol,’” study author Shoa Clarke of Stanford University said in a statement . “Or they say, ‘I changed my diet, and it had a huge effect on my cholesterol.’”

To find out why, Clarke and a team of medical researchers examined health data from a diverse group of nearly 21,000 postmenopausal women enrolled in the Women’s Health Initiative, a longitudinal national health study launched in 1991 that collected genetic profiles, dietary questionnaires, and blood lipid panels from the participants. Using a polygenic risk score established in a prior study, they found that those with a greater genetic predisposition to higher cholesterol were also more sensitive to saturated fat intake.

“Sometimes people think, ‘Oh, if I’m genetically prone to something, then it doesn’t really matter what my diet is or what the environment is like; it’s genetically predetermined.’ But what we’re saying here is the opposite,” Clarke explained. “The people who had this genetic predisposition for higher LDL were actually the ones with the most sensitivity to diet, where diet has the best chance of helping them—or hurting them, if the diet isn’t good.”

When the team looked at the incidence of adverse cardiovascular events among the women, the same pattern emerged. The top 25 percent of participants with a genetic bent toward high LDL levels who consumed more saturated fat were also more likely to suffer a heart attack, stroke, or other adverse cardiovascular event. The saturated fat intake for the remaining 75 percent didn’t seem to matter as much. “This variation in response to saturated fat may be one of the reasons there is so much controversy and disagreement over how much is okay in a diet,” Clarke said.

Of course, the study comes with some fine print. The food questionnaires were only given once, covering a three-month period in a longer study, so it’s entirely possible they changed over time. Additionally, only postmenopausal women were studied. The outcomes for men or women of different ages may vary.

But the bottom line is a familiar one (with a twist): reducing saturated fat is good for your LDL levels, especially if you’re genetically prone to high cholesterol.

items.title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
items.author: Shalma Wegsman
items.summary: The artist had no formal math education, yet as a new exhibition shows, the insights revealed in his artwork became an enduring inspiration to mathematicians. The post How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds first appeared on Quanta Magazine

Day and Night , February 1938, woodcut printed from two blocks, 15 3/8 x 26 5/8 in

M.C. Escher artwork ©The M.C. Escher Heritage. EscherSite collection.

M aurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

Escher saw that nature can sometimes produce impossible-seeming images. All around him, he saw distorted reflections, odd perspectives, and superimposed worlds, like the surface of a pond where you can see images of both the fish below and the trees reflected from above.

In rendering these and other visions, his artwork took on unmistakably mathematical qualities. “By keenly confronting the enigmas that surround us, and by considering and analyzing the observations that I had made, I ended up in the domain of mathematics,” he wrote in his introduction to the book M.C. Escher : The Graphic Work .

His journey among these enigmas is the subject of an exhibition entitled Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher at the National Museum of Mathematics (MoMath) in New York City.

Escher’s path toward math started with his love of tilings. After completing his arts education in 1922, Escher visited Granada, Spain, and was taken with the tile patterns that decorated the Alhambra. Inspired, he began to systematically study how to fill a sheet of paper with repeating shapes without leaving any gaps.

Years later, Escher’s half-brother, a geologist named Berend, sent him a paper by a mathematician named George Pólya. The paper categorized all the ways to cover a flat space with tiles, broken down into 17 groups, each with different symmetries. Escher had intuited a mathematical question, and here he had a mathematical answer.

Escher carefully traced the paper’s diagrams and studied them meticulously. Over time, he developed his own system for tessellating space, finding ways to cover a print with irregular shapes that resembled fish, birds, bats, lizards, and so on.

“He had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges,” said Doris Schattschneider, a mathematician and leading authority on Escher, and a curator of the exhibition.

Carolina MacGillavry, a Dutch crystallographer, took notice of Escher’s mastery of color symmetry — the rule ensuring that adjacent shapes in a tessellation are always different colors — and published a book in 1965 analyzing his drawings.

“[MacGillavry] realized that [Escher] knew more than all the crystallographers about color symmetry,” Schattschneider said. “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”

In 1954, his work was exhibited at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam. There, he was introduced to the geometer Harold Scott MacDonald (H.S.M.) Coxeter. The two exchanged letters until Escher’s death in 1972, and these exchanges inspired some of his most mathematically complex work.

items.title: Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works
items.author: Phillip Pyle
items.summary: The artist filed the complaint six months after terminating her relationship with dealer Richard Saltoun.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Phillip Pyle
Eleanor Antin Sues Dealer for Withholding Nearly 200 Works

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Conceptual artist Eleanor Antin is seeking the return of at least 179 works or $975,000 in compensatory damages in a lawsuit against her dealer, Richard Saltoun. The complaint was filed in New York State Supreme Court on July 29, six months after the artist terminated her relationship with Saltoun’s namesake gallery, which operates locations in New York, London, and Rome.

Filed by the 91-year-old artist’s son and attorney-in-fact, Blaise Antin, and her studio, Paranoid Productions, the suit claims that Saltoun “initially purported to agree to return all of the works it held” upon their business separation at the gallery's London location on January 16. News of the lawsuit was first reported by Artnet.

Saltoun claimed in February that the gallery had returned all of Antin’s works to her family, according to filed documents. However, later that month, the artist’s archivist, citing an inventory produced by Saltoun himself, allegedly discovered that Antin was still missing at least 179 works, the majority of which were still held at the London gallery.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This week, the Vilcek Foundation announced its third annual open call for grant applications. The organization invites nonprofits whose work aligns with the foundation’s mission to elevate immigrant contributions in the United States and foster an appreciation for the arts and sciences to apply for funding now through March 31, 2027. 

The foundation will award a total of $200,000 to US-based nonprofits as a part of its 2027 grants cycle. Individual organizations may apply for a grant of up to $20,000.

Applicants should lead innovative initiatives that generate measurable impact within and beyond their immediate communities. Strong applications demonstrate both a unique vision and clear plan of action for uplifting immigrants, the arts, or the sciences. Qualifying organizations must be recognized as tax-exempt under Section 501(c)(3). 

The Vilcek Foundation is actively expanding the geographic reach of its grantmaking with the goal of supporting organizations across all US states and select territories. The 2027 grant cycle aims to support nonprofits based around the country, including those in the following locations not previously represented in the foundation’s grantmaking: Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Iowa, Mississippi, Nevada, South Carolina, South Dakota, West Virginia, Wisconsin, American Samoa, Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

Since its founding in 2000, the Vilcek Foundation has remained steadfast in its philanthropic mission. To date, the foundation has provided more than $7 million in grants to nonprofits in 40 states, two US territories, and Washington, DC.

Earlier this month, the foundation announced the 12 organizations receiving funding as a part of its 2026 grants cycle. Situated across the country, the 2026 grantees include the Bemis Center for Contemporary Arts; Counterpublic, whose Triennial is currently on view in St. Louis; Delaware Contemporary Arts; and the Japanese American National Museum.

The 2027 Vilcek Foundation grant period will run from September 1, 2027 through August 31, 2028.

Organizations may apply for either project support or operating support. 

Interested nonprofits should submit applications via the foundation’s Grants Portal by 11:59 pm (ET) on March 31, 2027.

For full eligibility requirements and application details, visit vilcek.org/grants.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The world is full of tiny things that live off more charismatic hosts. Parasite ecologists say that these critters, too, are finally starting to get the conservation attention they deserve

Giardia lamblia parasite as Closup – 3D Rendering. High quality Rendering

This story was originally published by Knowable Magazine .

In the 1980s, biologists rounded up every last California condor for captive breeding. It was an unprecedented conservation project with stunning success: Today, the birds number more than 600 .

But for some ecologists, there’s a distressing corollary: The birds were reportedly treated with pesticides that killed condor parasites, including one unique to these birds , the condor louse Colpocephalum californici . The condor louse became a poster child for parasite extinction.

Parasites have a bad rap. But parasite ecologists say most parasitic species don’t harm us or our domestic animals and, in fact, make important contributions to life on Earth.

Amid today’s rapidly changing ecosystems, not much is known about how most parasites are faring: Better? Worse? The same? But by one estimate, climate-induced loss of habitat could cause extinction for 5 to 10 percent of parasite species by 2070. In 2023, the International Union for Conservation of Nature — the group responsible for the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species — started a new parasite specialist group , which aims to red-list more parasite species and develop conservation plans.

“They may be ugly; they might be gross,” says Chelsea Wood, a parasite ecologist at the University of Washington in Seattle. “But that doesn’t mean that they don’t have as much right to exist as any other species.”

Science has a strict definition for parasites: They live on or in their host, surviving at the host’s expense. But those host expenses vary. “Not all parasites have negative effects on their hosts all the time,” says Jason Weckstein, a bird and parasite expert at Drexel University in Philadelphia. There might be cases, for example, where a few parasites on an otherwise healthy critter might be no big deal, while a ton of parasites noshing on a sick, malnourished animal could be quite detrimental.

In many cases, parasites have coevolved with their hosts long enough to reach a truce. For example, humans have coexisted with parasitic worms for millennia, to the point that the worms can manage human immunity and metabolism in ways that might have benefits , like countering autoimmunity or allergies. That said, in high numbers, the same worms can cause severe disease, particularly in vulnerable people like children and pregnant women.

Beyond their hosts, parasites are members of the greater community . “It turns out that sucking blood and eating poo and all of the gross things that parasites do are really important functions in ecosystems,” says Wood. For example, like predators, parasites can keep animal populations in check.

Consider the flatworm Euhaplorchis californiensis , which cycles from snails to fish to birds . The California killifish it infects normally hide in the shadows. But with E. californiensis in their brains, the fish venture into unprotected waters, flash their shiny scales and are promptly gobbled by birds. The parasite takes the next step in its life cycle — and keeps energy and resources moving along the marsh’s food web.

Parasite action on ecosystems benefits humans, too, says Skylar Hopkins, a parasite ecologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh. For example, parasitoid wasps inject their eggs into other insects, including hosts that eat our crops. When invasive cassava mealybugs threatened African farms in the 1970s, introducing parasitoid wasp cocoons on land and by airdrop saved the harvest, ensuring that millions of people had enough to eat.

So parasites are important — but scientists are largely in the dark about how they’ll fare as hosts are threatened, humans encroach on wild areas and the climate changes. “We have, just barely, the foggiest clue about which parasites are likely to be endangered,” says Wood.

items.author: Miri Ahn
items.summary: Zadie Xa is a London-based multidisciplinary artist from Vancouver, Canada, whose practice spans painting, textiles, sound, installation, and performance. Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories,... The post The Stories of Clothes: An I

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Zadie Xa is a London-based multidisciplinary artist from Vancouver, Canada, whose practice spans painting, textiles, sound, installation, and performance. Her work explores questions of diasporic identity, belonging and cultural heritage, often engaging with spiritual histories, and folklore.

For the second iteration of New Work: The Stories of Clothes at V&A East Museum, Xa presents Amulets, a textile installation of seven jackets that gradually transform in scale and form. Inspired by traditional ceremonial garments and contemporary streetwear, the commission explores how clothing can communicate identity, and embody power.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the questions or ideas that guide your work?

In my practice I am interested in exploring ideas of placehood, belonging and identity through interspecies relations, spiritual histories, and the preservation and evolution of folk traditions.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shaped your vision?

I studied painting during both my undergraduate and master’s degrees, but eventually moved beyond conventional painting to engage directly with the materials and forms I had been referencing, like music and clothing. This led me to experiment with live performance and later with installation.

The transition from painting to a multidisciplinary practice came naturally to me. My approach to texture, colour and materials has been shaped by rifling through racks of clothing and shelves of knick-knacks in vintage shops as a teenager, as well as by my interest in music and sampling.

Rather than representing these influences solely through painting, I began incorporating them directly into my work. This has led me towards a more expansive way of working, opening up my practice to new materials and disciplines.

I am also deeply inspired by traditional clothing from around the world. I especially love the stories communities share through their regalia. This is also why I find music, and particularly sampling culture within hip-hop and pop music, so interesting.

Across disciplines, I use references to convey political ideas, pay homage and explore what emerges when contemporary forms meet historical traditions. This mixing relates to my own interest in hybridity and third-culture identities.

The commission is a textile installation comprising seven jackets suspended in a row, as if in procession. Each garment increases in scale from the first to the seventh, with the jackets connected as though growing and shapeshifting from one form or style into another.

How did you begin developing this work? What was your starting point?

My starting point was a site visit to V&A East, where I encountered a striking Daoist robe that became a key reference point.

I have long been interested in religious, spiritual and traditional regalia, particularly how their construction and printed or embroidered imagery communicate the wearer’s identity, local history, beliefs and political status.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In summer 2025, Sian Fan was selected as a Design Trust Fellow at V&A East . Her proposed project was to travel for the first time to Hong Kong and the New Territories to trace her Hakka family history and to search through the V&A’s collection for objects relating to her heritage.

As an artist as well as a contemporary and aerial dancer, Sian creates sculpture, costume, performance, animation, installation, and new media which is often informed by her questioning of her mixed Hakka Chinese and British identity.

Here Sian shares with us tales of her field research and the making of her new commission, The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) , which is on show in Gallery 3 of V&A East Storehouse.

Can you describe how your research began at V&A East Storehouse?

My research involved attempting to trace my familial journey as a Hakka descendant. As with many migrant stories it is punctured with gaps, holes and voids and I wanted to use the research to reframe these absences as opportunities for the creation of speculative stories.

Considering how in my and in many migrant families there is an absence of heirlooms and of tangible objects that connect with one’s family history, I wanted to embrace the V&A collections as a huge archive of proxy heirlooms. I was particularly inspired by the Liangmao hat as well as by Hakka textiles which are incredibly resourceful and make careful and attentive use of scraps of available fabrics. I’ve also taken inspiration from the Chinese embroidery within the collection.

And how was your field research in Hong Kong and the New Territories of Hong Kong and Fujian?

For my field research I visited Hong Kong and China for the first time. I spent time exploring the cityscape of Hong Kong, being immersed in the hectic and humid streets and visiting the different art organisations based there. I also visited heritage museums where I learnt about the cultural traditions of Hong Kong and Hakka people. In the New Territories of Hong Kong, I visited a friend’s Hakka village and attended a celebration for the re-opening of the village temple where there were lion dances, firecrackers and poon choi. I also hiked through rural New Territories to Kop Tong, my family’s ancestral village and found the abandoned house that my mum grew up in, before she left Hong Kong for England as a child.

Here I was able to glimpse and attempt to piece together her fragments of memories from her time there and it was a powerful and surreal experience. I discovered a small museum in the nearby Lai Chi Wo village that had information on the area that included information on my family as well as reconstructions of a Hakka style home, which jogged some of my mum’s memories when I later showed them to her. In Fujian I visited several Toulou buildings, which are a traditional form of Hakka architecture, which are usually circular structures with an open courtyard in the centre.

Can you describe your commission for V&A East Storehouse?

The commission is called The Body is a Relic (how the light gets in) . It is an installation consisting of three suspended body-like, life-sized sculptures representing a small family unit. The bodies have rounded bamboo frames, which are covered in different textured fabrics with differing opacities. Their heads appear as if wrapped in branches or vines, and the space where the head and neck would be is a cut-out, negative space. Strung vertically inside each body is a glowing light bar, which shines through the differing materials, revealing shapes within the layers, making the bodies akin to lanterns.

The textured materials feature images captured over the research trip rendered via embroidery and weaving. These images range from cut out wall features from traditional Hakka architecture, the patterned glass windowpane of my mother’s childhood home, the ornamental koi within one of the toulous and the lion dancers from the village celebrations. These are layered, distorted and reconfigured to create an abstract tapestry that reimagines memories, histories and stories.

The bamboo structures reference Hong Kong’s famous bamboo scaffold and the branch like structure of the figures’ heads is inspired by the winding branches that I encountered hiking to my ancestral village. The negative space of the body references the oculus like voids within the toulou houses and the opening for the head in the lian mao hats. In both of these examples, the empty space is filled with the body, filled with life.

Conceptually the work meditates upon disjointed histories and speculative story making, weaving together tales both real and imagined with equal value as a method of asserting agency over one’s historic and cultural identity, enabling a sense of belonging and dreaming into reality new states of self. The work explores how in the absence of heirlooms, tangible histories and family stories that the body is a tangible and meaningful record: the body itself is a relic.

items.title: The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with R.I.P. Germain
items.author: Miri Ahn
items.summary: R.I.P. Germain is a LA-based multidisciplinary artist born in Luton. His practice examines Black experience, identity and cultural history For the second iteration of New Work, The Stories of Clothes, Germain draws on his experience... The post The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with R.I.P. Germain appeared first on

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
R.I.P. Germain is a LA-based multidisciplinary artist born in Luton. His practice examines Black experience, identity and cultural history

For the second iteration of New Work , The Stories of Clothes , Germain draws on his experience of moving from the UK to Los Angeles and becoming more acutely aware of the highly specific meanings attached to clothing in different parts of the city. As a large Black man, he recognises that particular colours, brands or styles could lead others to associate him with a local gang, potentially placing him in danger. Clothing therefore became more than a form of personal expression. It operated as a social code through which identity, affiliation and threat could be read or misread.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the questions or ideas that guide your work?

Unruly fukkry. That’s where my head’s at right now with my practice. I’m really enjoying creating with this mindstate. It’s liberating. I’m not concerned with whether the works I’m making are gallery friendly or institutional…at all. To meet me, think of it like this, there are five questions that I cycle through constantly during the process of making a work. They sort of act like five pendants hung on my chain (practice).

These questions have become a mantra – they keep me focused, and on the right path. Rigid and fluid.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shaped your vision?

‘Brixton Quincey talks doing Black Magic (Juju) & Shoot out (Part 5) #OFTR’ – LSL FILMS

‘good kid, m.A.A.d city – A Short Film by Kendrick Lamar’ – Kendrick Lamar

In that order. That’ll give you a little bit of insight into where I’ve come from.

wheeloffortune is a horror agent. It is art imitating aspects of my life and riffing off of it. The film consists of a slideshow of polaroids of individual items of clothing as well as configurations of said clothes, that can be and have been used as signals of kinship, as well as acts of war in Los Angeles, depending on where you find yourself in the city, and if you’re Black or Brown. Aesthetic languages from the high end luxury streetwear industry, African American Angeleno gangbanging culture, and crime scene forensics are interwoven to visualise a long period of ponderment from myself about trying to come to terms with being a walking target, being seen as a threat, being considered a threat and being treated as a threat. You might think those last three things are similar, but they are not! The threat of danger is completely different between the three. wheeloffortune is not meant to have answers for the questions I’m posing with it, it is a very much needed act of respite, and a peek through another lens into the absurdities of modern Americana and the constant hum of terror that it manages to impose on the people that live in the US.

How did you begin developing this work? What was your starting point?

A near death experience. It sprouts from there. It’s one of two byproducts of a clarity of thought from a period of reflection.

What was your process like for researching and making this commission?

I wouldn’t even attempt to try to figure out how many hours I spent sourcing the clothes that were used in wheeloffortune . I remember it taking me five months of consistent searching on the internet in secondary clothing marketplaces to find one fitted hat. Every piece of clothing in the film is either something an African American gangbanger in Los Angeles would actually wear to show their affiliation to their gang, or it features a reference and/or symbol that with artistic licence on my part, could be worn by a gang member to show their allegiance to a specific gang. One example of that artistic licence being used would be that the yellow pieces of clothing that feature in the film are meant to result in an outfit that a member of the Main Street Mafia Crips could wear. So, because they wear clothes that typically sport an “M” logo on them of some kind, and the clothes are either blue, yellow or both in colour, such as the Michigan Wolverines fitted cap, I bought a quite rare collaborative hoodie between Palace and McDonalds, and a pair of Evisu Daicock Print #2000 Baggy-Fit Jeans, because they both have a yellow “M” looking logo blasted on them. This attention to detail has been applied to every item of clothing. There is some type of lore attached to all of them, whether that be through the difficulty in me acquiring them and/or the history attached to the item of clothing itself in relation to the fashion world.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Industrial Designers Jimin Jeon and Adam Huxley Khng have been working together since they met in Tokyo in 2019. The duo were selected as inaugural Design Trust Fellows in 2025. They have been researching garment fasteners within the V&A’s collection as well as in Hong Kong and China.

Here Adam and Jimin share with us their research journey and how they developed their final commissioned installation on display in Gallery 1 of V&A East Storehouse: Motions and Notions of Fastening.

Can you describe the research you conducted as part of the Design Trust Fellowship?

Adam: Our research focused on garment fastenings and the recurring gestures and forms associated with them. We became interested in the actions and principles that have accompanied fastening technologies from prehistory to the present day, and the ways those forms have evolved through continuous refinement and adaptation.

We started with the idea that fastenings are much more than functional mechanisms or decorative details. They fundamentally shape the architecture and construction of clothing. Drawing on our background in industrial design, we became interested in understanding how fastenings have been conceived, developed and manufactured over time, and how they might continue to evolve in the future.

Jimin: One idea that became particularly important to us was what we described as an investigative process. When you encounter a museum object, you are often given information such as its materials, dimensions or date, but there is so much that remains unknown. You don’t necessarily know how it was used, how it felt to handle, or what role it played in everyday life. That absence of information becomes productive. It invites speculation and reflection.

Jimin: The ability to handle objects during our research time at the V&A East Storehouse was incredibly important. For example, when we examined a jade belt hook, the catalogue could tell us what it was and roughly when it was made, but it couldn’t communicate the experience of holding it. The moment you pick it up, you feel its weight. You notice the temperature of the jade. You hear the subtle sound made when the pieces connect. Those qualities don’t exist in photographs or catalogue records. They can only be understood through direct experience. That kind of encounter became one of the most valuable parts of the project.

How did the opportunity to research in Hong Kong, China and the Greater Bay Area influence your practice?

Adam: The trip gave us a much broader understanding of production. We weren’t just interested in individual products; we wanted to understand the entire journey of an object, from manufacture and distribution through to sale and use. One of the most striking experiences was visiting manufacturing centres where huge quantities of fastenings are produced. You start to see how a seemingly small component can have enormous significance within a local economy and a much wider global network.

Jimin: Meeting people was equally important. There was a remarkable sense of immediacy and openness. Someone would say, “Do you want to see this?” and suddenly you were being introduced to another manufacturer or another part of the production process. Trust and personal connections played a significant role in how knowledge and expertise moved through the industry.

Adam: When we began the project, we expected to discover dramatic technological change. We found that, of course. But what surprised us was how much had remained the same. Many of the fundamental principles of fastening have changed very little over thousands of years. What has changed are the methods of production, the contexts in which objects operate, and the networks through which they circulate. That continuity between past and present became one of the most important discoveries of the project.

How did you approach classifying the garment fasteners you were researching?

Jimin: Instead of categorising fastenings according to their appearance or historical period, we started classifying them according to action and movement. Gradually, three primary categories emerged.

The first was piercing : materials joined through penetration, such as pins, brooches or other forms that hold materials together by passing through them.

Bringing together people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities, ELTA creates ambitious collaborative textile... The post The Stories of Clothes: An Interview with Ea

items.cleanReaderHtml:
East London Textile Arts (ELTA) is a Newham-based, artist-led community textile collective that has been working with local communities since 2007. Bringing together people of different ages, backgrounds and abilities, ELTA creates ambitious collaborative textile projects rooted in long-term relationships, shared creativity and the belief that art should be accessible to everyone.

Since the early development of V&A East, ELTA has been a collective we have wanted to work with. Its longstanding commitment to Newham’s communities, and its approach to textiles as a way of expressing personal and collective experiences, resonate closely with V&A East’s ambitions.

For the second iteration of New Work: The Stories of Clothes , ELTA has created a new installation exploring what people love and fear. Developed with members of the collective and local community groups, the commission brings together embroidered garments, photography and a large circular patchwork skirt, transforming a public space into a celebration of collective creativity and the stories that clothes can tell.

We spoke with Celia and Sonia, who lead ELTA, about their practice, creative process, and the experiences behind this new commission.

Can you briefly describe your practice and the ideas that guide your work?

Celia: ELTA’s members are ethnically diverse, mostly women, older and on low incomes. Many have health conditions or disabilities, and many speak English as an additional language. Over 25% of the collective have learning disabilities, with members ranging in age from their 20s to their early 60s.

We believe that high-quality textiles can be made within non-professional communities that have a long-term vision. ELTA works collectively and focuses on building lasting creative relationships with communities in Newham, rather than treating each project as a separate, one-off activity.

How did you come to work this way? What are particular moments, influences or experiences that shape your vision?

Celia: I came to work this way after spending three years in Bucharest, Romania, where I was greatly influenced by the Muzeul Naţional al Ţăranului Român (National Museum of the Romanian Peasant) and its director during the 1990s, Horia Bernea, who redesigned the museum after the collapse of communism.

He transformed it into a space that focused on craftwork made by people as part of their daily lives, work not generally thought of as ‘art’. The museum’s design, with its hand-painted walls and refusal to give space to marketing posters, gave it a unity and purpose: to celebrate the gifts and lives of Romanian people. I was also inspired by its political purpose, to reconsider what it meant to be human in a post-communist world.

Other influences include non-professional ‘village’ textiles, such as those of the Rabari communities in Gujarat, Romanian village textiles, and various textile NGOs established in India, Pakistan and Bangladesh to develop and sell embroidery and other handcrafted textiles.

When I arrived in Newham from Romania in 2005, I was struck by the vibrant colours of the many Asian textile shops, the different festivals and street processions. Everywhere there were the most colourful and varied textiles and clothes. It made me want to drop painting and join this party of cloth.

Sonia: I met Celia in 2007 and, having an interest in embroidery, I joined the project. I went on to teach and design with groups, collaborating with Celia on project development.

Celia: Our commission for the V&A is a wall installation comprising 9 kaftans, one quilt, one scarf, thirteen photographs and one crazy patchwork hanging/skirt.

items.author: Georgia Haseldine

Her practice is eclectic – moving between photography, textile, sculpture, video and... The post The Stories of Clothes: An interview with Alia Ali appeared first on V&A Blog .

Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Arist Alia Ali works with light, language and architecture, as these are the tools she sees us understand and construct worlds around us. Her practice is eclectic – moving between photography, textile, sculpture, video and installation work – and often works across borders, travelling for her artworks to the source of materials and craft skills she wants to explore.

In 2025, Ali joined the V&A as the Jameel Fellow and investigated objects in the collection which attested to the material culture of the Indian Ocean world with her home-country of Yemen at its centre. Her research informed her newly commissioned installation at the V&A East Museum, Portable Sanctuaries: 3000 years ago/Now/3000 years forward . Here Ali shares with us her insights into the V&A’s collection and why and how her new commission was created.

‘Hand and Land’ are two guiding principles for your work – can you explain this?

There is the land: plants, animals, minerals, water, soil, metals, stones. And there is the hand. Between them exist centuries, sometimes millennia, of knowledge.

I am less interested in asking someone, “Where are you from?” because I am not sure geography alone can answer that question. I am more interested in asking: What do your hands make? What land has sustained you? What do you wear? What do you carry? What have you inherited? What protects you? What travels with you even when it cannot be seen?

These are also the questions I take into my research with objects. For example, cloth is never simply decorative. It carries histories of movement, trade, colonisation, labour, belief and exchange. It can travel enormous distances while retaining evidence of everywhere it has been. A pattern can migrate. A dye can migrate. A technique can migrate. A word can migrate. A person can migrate. None necessarily arrives unchanged, but neither does it entirely leave behind where it came from. But cloth is also extraordinarily intimate. We wrap ourselves in it. We sleep in it. We protect ourselves with it. We inherit it. We carry it when we move.

What was the starting point for your research as part of the Jameel Fellowship?

I wanted to understand Yemen through its millennia-long participation in the Indian Ocean world, and through the histories of the places with which it has exchanged ideas, materials, people, language and belief: India, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Malaysia, what is now Singapore, Zanzibar, Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, Oman and many others. Yemen begins to look very different when it is understood through water rather than through continental borders. It is so often imagined externally through desert and land, but I relate to Yemen very strongly through water and mountains. Its history is profoundly maritime. I began thinking about Yemen as something much more Afro–Indo–Arab than what can be contained within a purely continental understanding of West Asia or the Middle East.

I spent three months working within the V&A’s Asia Department, guided particularly by Rachel Dedman, Jameel Curator of Contemporary Art from the Middle East, and in conversation with curators working across different parts of Asia and different material histories, including fashion and textiles. I also spent an extraordinary amount of time in V&A East Storehouse, in the stacks and collections, simply looking, guided by Georgia Haseldine, Senior Curator, V&A East Storehouse. Alongside this, through the V&A’s Cultures in Crisis programme with Laura Searson, I began exploring conflict as a starting point rather than an endpoint: how to break from the dystopic narratives that so often surround places marked by conflict, and instead look through the past, including the nostalgia we attach to it, as a way of giving space to reimagined futures.

I was drawn to objects that sat somewhere between beauty, belief, danger, protection, adornment and the body. They came from very different times, geographies and material worlds, and many of them would probably never ordinarily be placed beside one another. What became interesting to me was allowing those objects to speak across those distances. An ancient talismanic garment could sit in my mind alongside a contemporary dress. An object made to carry something close to the body could speak to an object intended to protect it. Creatures, language, minerals, textiles and forms began to create relationships that were not necessarily there when I first encountered them.

Some of these objects I’ve put together into a display at V&A East Storehouse.

The fellowship fundamentally changed my relationship to geography and time. Looking deeply at objects from the past made me realise that I wasn’t particularly interested in history simply as something to recover or look back upon. It became material through which I could look forward.

I began thinking about approximately 3,000 years behind us and imagining 3,000 years ahead. If these languages, materials, stories, creatures, symbols, plants, minerals and relationships have travelled thousands of years to reach us, then I want the work to insist upon their right to continue travelling. To me, that insistence is radical.

The future does not have to mean abandoning the earth or the knowledge that brought us here. It doesn’t have to mean colonising the constellations. Perhaps imagining the future requires us to understand more deeply what has already sustained us.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Burbot ( Lota lota ), better known as cusk in northern New England, are usually green or brown, but the specimen just plucked out of Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario is somehow a bright shade of yellow.

It was discovered by biologists from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), who describe it as a “one-in-a-million” catch. The yellow hue is brought on by a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism, which suppresses red pigmentation to leave yellow at the fore. It can happen in birds and amphibians, as well as fish.

Read more: “ Scientists Catch a Rare Glimpse of a Fish With a See-Through Head ”

Making the catch even more notable is that burbot usually live in colder, deeper waters. That it was found in a harbor with a maximum depth of 27 feet is unusual, though it’s not clear why or how it got lost. It’s the first time a burbot of any color has been picked up in Oswego Harbor.

The fish was found by the Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program run by the USFWS, which looks for aquatic species that are somewhere they shouldn’t be in terms of ecosystem health. The program uses methods like electrofishing (stunning fish with electricity), fyke-netting (tubular traps), gill-netting (walled nets), and environmental DNA analysis on water samples to identify what’s in rivers, lakes, and oceans.

When it comes to monitoring Lake Ontario and other bodies of water, it’s important that invasive species can be quickly detected and removed at an early stage.

Burbot is a native fish in this area, but it continues to struggle in terms of population numbers, mostly due to the parasitic, invasive sea lamprey. This particular yellow specimen was sick as well and taken away to Cornell University for further testing. It’s possible that its bright yellow coloring has been something of a disadvantage when it comes to sneaking up on other fish for food.

The hope is that the testing gives experts more clues about why burbot numbers remain low around Lake Ontario.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The Argentine physicist Gabriel Mindlin has spent much of his career researching how birds learn to sing. He focuses on the rufous-collared sparrow ( Zonotrichia capensis ), a species common across urban and suburban Argentina, where it’s often called a ‘chingolo’. As in other songbirds, the male’s song is not innate but passed down from adult males to younger ones, who sing it throughout their lives to guard territory and find a mate.

In this short documentary, the Argentine director Martín Benchimol chronicles Mindlin’s latest breakthrough. Comparing the songs of today’s chingolos with those transcribed by hand in the 1960s, Mindlin realised that some melodies had survived the decades while others had disappeared. Using mathematical models, he and his team set out to revive the vanished songs and teach them back to living birds. With a cinematic eye, Benchimol follows the researchers as they attempt an audacious act of cultural engineering, building robotic song tutors, planting them in the wild and tracking whether young birds pick up these lost tunes.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 presidential election, I was in the last place I wanted to be: Washington, DC. Where would I go? I wanted nothing to do with his administration’s empty grandeur. I spent the day at Maya Lin’s Vietnam War Memorial, a dark wound in the earth. In this much more hopeful moment post-midterms, Ed Simon asks a related question: How should memorials remember the MAGA era? He points to historical anti-fascist examples in Germany — and also suggests the bulldozing of Trump’s ballroom to rubble as its own kind of monument. 

Satire’s not a bad strategy to record this era, either. Also today, Greg Werkheiser pens an obituary for the National Historic Preservation Act. The act’s next of kin, the National Register of Historic Places, he writes, “is said to be concerned about its own health.”

Finally, don’t miss the newest installation of Jennifer Samet’s “Beer With a Painter” column. She interviews Ivorian painter Ouattara Watts, who works only at night, when the veil between this world and the next is thinnest. Plus, The Met and the Shanghai Museum are teaming up, just weeks after MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Museum joined forces. They say art imitates life; I just didn’t know that meant we were getting museum oligopolies.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy. | Ed Simon

items.title: The Directing Genius of Akira Kurosawa Explained
items.author: Colin Marshall
items.summary: Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa, but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa, but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, Throne of Blood, The Bad Sleep Well, and Ran were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from The Magnificent Seven and A Fistful of Dollars in the nineteen-sixties to Living and Highest 2 Lowest in this decade.

Nor can it be a coincidence that the appreciative voices opening the StudioBinder video on Kurosawa’s genius above belong to Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, and George Lucas. Yet this most internationally celebrated of all Japanese filmmakers can’t, ultimately, have been just a Westerner in disguise, since his work gives viewers around the world something that their domestic movies don’t.

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said, expressing his dedication to the ideal of (as no less an American auteur than Jerry Lewis described himself) the total filmmaker.

That Kurosawa understood how to tell a story in a way that transcends cultural boundaries goes without saying; what’s less widely appreciated is the way he did so with a combination of simplicity and complexity. As he put it, “a truly good movie is interesting and easy to understand,” two qualities that often end up in irresolvable tension, at least in the hands of lesser filmmakers. Even among those influenced by Kurosawa, for example, some have mastered immediate visual legibility without ever understanding that sound and music are more effectively used as a counterpoint to, rather than mere intensification of, a scene’s prevailing emotion. How many living directors, for that matter, convincingly approach grand, universal themes without irony or protective distance? If Kurosawa’s films retain a power that seems inaccessible today, it may be because, for him, there was no East or West: there was only cinema.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Earlier this month, Salon announced that it’s ceasing publication after 31 years. In its farewell address, the magazine writes: “The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.” We can sympathize.

Over the 20 years we have served you, we have watched quality websites come and go. Some once-vibrant sites have gone entirely dark. Today, if you want to sift through the remains of the early internet, you can head over to the Internet Archive—a site that “captures and stores over one trillion web pages to safeguard digital history and prevent the rewriting or erasure of online records.” In the case of Salon, the Internet Archive has launched Salon Explorer, a “new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism.” According to a new blog post from the Internet Archive, the tool lets you browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers, with filters that make it easier to find stories you may have missed. If it isn’t your preferred interface, you can also browse Salon.com using the Wayback Machine. RIP Salon, long live the Internet Archive.

Enter the Salon Explorer here.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic's writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us.

Hilma af Klint Work Heads to Auction

Works by the Swedish spiritualist and abstract art pioneer, who asked that her paintings remain unseen for 20 years after her death in 1944, have not come up for auction in more than three decades. That's about to change with the emergence of “Ser III No. 5” (1920) at the Stockholm-based house Bukowskis, which estimates the oil and graphite on canvas will fetch up to 8 million SEK (~$791,000) in its upcoming November 18–19 sale. Controversy has long followed the legacy of the late artist, with some arguing that her works should be kept together rather than sold and commercialized.

Sotheby's Settles Dispute With Heirs Who Contested Van Gogh Sale

After the heirs of the Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer requested the withdrawal of Van Gogh's “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (1890) from a sale at Sotheby's, claiming that the work had been sold under duress amid Nazi persecution in Europe, the family has reached a “mutually satisfactory resolution” with the work's consignors, said a Sotheby's statement shared with Hyperallergic. But will the dispute put a damper on sale results? We'll find out tomorrow night when the painting, valued at $180 million, goes under the hammer.

items.author: Jake Currie
items.summary: Deepfakes have jumped the uncanny valley The post What Goes on in Our Brains When We See an AI Face appeared first on Nautilus .

images.caption: Lámina de Nautilus

items.cleanReaderHtml:
AI artificial intelligence or female programmer coder – binary computer code superimposed on face of woman

Gone are the days when we could make fun of AI-generated faces for grotesque errors like mangled cauliflower ears and an inhuman number of teeth. A steady stream of advancements now allow the technology to manufacture faces that look real. A little too real, according to a new study published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience .

Psychologists from the University of Florida recruited over 150 participants—some young (18 to 37), some old (60 to 89)—to find out how their brains responded to seeing faces generated by AI. The participants were shown photos featuring either actual human faces or AI-generated faces and asked to rate how realistic they were on a scale from 1 to 10, all while their brains were scanned by an fMRI machine.

Remarkably, both groups rated the faces concocted by computers as more realistic than the actual faces of honest-to-god human beings. “Fake faces are being perceived as more real than real faces,” study author Natalie Ebner said in a statement . “You’re actually worse than just guessing, because you’re actively being drawn in the wrong direction.”

When they viewed AI faces, the participants’ brains showed muted activity in the anterior insula. Tucked inside the Sylvian fissure (the deep crease in the side of the brain), this neural region is responsible for processing untrustworthy cues. The relatively diminished activity suggests the hyperreal faces weren’t triggering any neural alarms, the researchers say.

According to the team, we perceive AI faces as hyperreal because they’re essentially an average of lots of faces. Distinctive features have been sanded off, and the result is something prototypical, attractive, and familiar—and we find familiar faces more trustworthy. In other words, AI faces may have leapt over the uncanny valley.

There was one other interesting wrinkle. Even though their brain activity didn’t differ significantly, older people tended to believe AI faces were more real than their younger counterparts. While both groups rated actual faces similarly, older adults rated AI faces 1.11 points more realistic, compared to just 0.25 points for younger folks. “All adults have hyperrealism bias, not just older adults,” Ebner said. “But older adults have it more.”

It’s not entirely clear why, however. It could be because older people tend to lean on the familiar more in general or that they’re less aware about AI-generated deepfakes, the researchers said. Either way it makes them attractive targets for scams. “Identifying that this potential deception scheme is the first step to an intervention,” Ebner said. “We can now work on awareness that if something looks too good to be true, think twice before you go along with it.”

Of course, raising awareness is easier said than done in an information environment already rife with scams.

items.title: How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?
items.author: Ed Simon
items.summary: Anti-monumentalism responds not with grand equestrian statues or neoclassical columns, but with absence and anxiety, minimalism and melancholy.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Ed Simon
How Should We Memorialize the Trump Era?

items.cleanReaderHtml:
At the intersection of the Harburger Ring and Sand Street in Hamburg, Germany, there is a most unusual public memorial, visible only to those who already know what they’re looking for.

When the “Monument Against Fascism” was unveiled in 1986, it was a 40-foot-tall (~12.2 m) rectangular aluminum pillar covered in lead sheeting on which Hamburg residents were invited to inscribe their own pledges to fight authoritarianism. Over the next seven years, the column was lowered into the ground in stages, so that today the monument is entirely subterranean, visible only through a small glass window next to the plaque.

Designed by married conceptual artists Esther Shalev-Gerz and Jochen Gerz and commissioned by the Municipal Council of Hamburg-Harburg, the monument was intended to confront both Germany’s Nazi past and the reemergence of far-right politics in a provocative, arresting manner that purposefully eschewed the monumental architecture that fascists themselves exalted. The result was Shalev-Gerz and Gerz’s consummate anti-monument, a reminder that the war against fascism is as personal as someone’s handwriting and as continual as the ground beneath our feet.

items.author: Rhea Nayyar
items.summary: With work by Shahzia Sikander and Hylozoic/Desires, “Between Salt and Smoke” simultaneously probes and defies the violent and extractive legacies of British imperialism across Asia.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Smoke presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires.

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty.

The end of the year is quickly approaching, and you know what that means: gifting season is here.

Like clockwork, we’re back with a carefully curated, handy dandy gift guide to help you pick out the perfect presents for each name on your list. Organized by passions and personalities, our list has something special for everyone. So sit back, brew a cup of tea, and get scrolling! You’re about to have the breeziest holiday shopping yet.

As always, thank you for supporting Colossal.

For the Creative Professional

Visual thinkers understand the absolute joy of impeccably designed things. Treat the creative in your life to studio essentials that make the workday lighter and intriguing reads to keep the ideas flowing.

More is more! If bold colors, clashing patterns, and whimsical graphics are that special someone’s vibe, we’ve got the perfect accessories to complete their closet.

We all know someone who feels the happiest among flora, fauna, and the great outdoors. Bring a bit of nature to them with a new pair of gardening gloves, fungi-inspired decor and puzzles, a guide to foraging for handmade inks, and plenty more.

For the Tasteful Host

Those with great taste often have a cozy home to match. Help your favorite host make their space even warmer with aesthetically-pleasing objects for cooking, gathering, and lingering just a bit longer.

For the Serial Hobbyist

Our exciting range of craft kits open up a world of possibilities for those who never seem to get tired of trying new hobbies. From hand loom weaving and embroidery to pressing flowers and growing herbs, there’s something new to try for everyone.

For the Budding Artist

What’s more important than encouraging those just beginning to explore their creative side? Surprise that little one with a big imagination with specially-crafted wooden toys, beautiful books, unique crayons, and beyond.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
There’s a spot in southern Saudi Arabia where you can find seashells in the middle of the desert. Roughly 125,000 years ago, a 130-square-mile portion of the Najran Province was covered in around 100 feet of freshwater (give or take, depending on the year’s rainfall). This prehistoric lake (called Mundafan) was surrounded by lush wetlands where palms and reeds thrived, feeding a menagerie of large herbivores like extinct long-horned buffalo, ostrich, and hippopotamuses. According to a new study published in Science , prehistoric humans hunted these animals, and they used some surprisingly sophisticated Stone Age technology to do it.

An international team of archaeologists excavating the site found more than 5,500 stone artifacts that paint a picture of how archaic humans living on the lakeshores used the lake’s bounty to their benefit. The smooth surfaces of stone-cutting implements showed evidence of plant material like cucumber relatives and cattails, while neatly serrated edges contained “exceptionally well preserved” fibers from palm leaves. According to the team, the finds indicate the lakeside populations didn’t just eat the plants, but transformed them into other useful items, like cordage, bindings, and matting.

Read more: “ Ice Age Spear Points Tell a Fascinating Story of Human Progress ”

Among the stone artifacts were over 130 fossilized bone fragments from hippos, antelope, gazelles and more, as well as over 100 ostrich egg-shell fragments. The mix of water-dwelling and dry-country fauna indicates the lake was likely surrounded by savannas. While the bones themselves didn’t show signs of butchery, the close proximity to the stone tools and the density of the find suggests they were food.

“The paleolake was therefore not simply a source of drinking water and prey but an ecological focus around which varied technological and subsistence activities were organized,” the researchers wrote.

So how did these prehistoric hunters bring down hippo-sized prey?

Per an analysis of the stone spear tips it might not have been a fair fight. On the hafts (the portion attached to the shaft of the spear), the team found residue from plant adhesives. On the tips, they found toxins from the arrow poison tree. Similar to the toxins from Digitalis (foxglove), these cardiac glycosides can decrease the heart rate and may have given our prehistoric ancestors a lethal edge in bringing down the massive beasts. (Fun fact: The African maned rat also uses poison from the tree, covering its fur in the toxic substance to ward off predators.)

It might not be the most sporting way to hunt, but it is ingenious.

Our early human ancestors telling fireside stories may have propelled the development of speech by facilitating discussion of more abstract concepts

Deep in a phantasmagorical cave, a gathering of uncanny figures and critters emerges from dark waters in the music video for “Janjan” by alternative K-pop group Balming Tiger. Both playful and a little eerie, the animated work celebrates collectivity and freedom of expression.

Directed and animated by Takahashi Riku, a.k.a. DOKUZEN, the surreal music video is composed predominantly of stop-motion scenes set to a thumping rhythm to which fantastical paper figures dance as if performing esoteric rituals. It also features an interlude of drawn animations—a kind of world within a world.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Whether showcasing a prized possession or peering through a spyglass to navigate open water, Juliet Schreckinger’s curious characters work together and form unexpected alliances. Personalities like Oscar the Octopus and Quinn the Sperm Whale recur in the artist’s ink and graphite drawings, and her most recent series comprises the show Limitless Sea at Arch Enemy Arts.

Schreckinger’s marine and woodland critters adopt a playful, cartoonish air, like personalities in a children’s book who find themselves adrift and in need of a friend. Lighthouses, lanterns, and rays of sun breaking through clouds glow with optimism. And while an overarching narrative may be murky, the unlikely companions and cooperative activities illuminate dreamlike scenes that encourage inquisitiveness and joy.

An undercurrent of persistence and hope also runs through Limited Sea, mirroring the artist’s recent healing process after a major surgery. It’s “a show made up of characters navigating through the foggy darkness by focusing on the light…and on the other side is limitless possibility,” Schreckinger says in a statement. As she navigated her own challenges—including making this series with only one good eye—these works served as a reminder of what’s most important: “finding the beauty, finding the light, and spending time with those who make your soul happy,” she says.

Limitless Sea continues through November 29 in Philadelphia. Schreckinger’s work will also be on view next month in General Strike 2, an exhibition of artist matchboxes, at Joy Machine. See more on Schreckinger’s Instagram.

At a café in downtown Tehran, Iran, on 11 September 2026. Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/via Getty Images

is an Iranian writer who lives in Paris, France. Her work has appeared in The New Statesman , BBC Persian, Euronews Persian as well as in Iranian journals.

Yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the new fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth and smudgy pink eyeshadow extending beyond the corner of each eye. She tells her followers that, before she leaves her house, her mother says: ‘Put on less makeup.’ ‘Mum, be reasonable,’ she answers. ‘I’m going to Iranshahr. For Iranshahr this is nothing. I’m going to Paris Fashion Week. You know everyone there is doing a catwalk.’

Iranshahr’s sidewalks teem with young people parading the latest fashions and filming other young, stylish people for their social media feeds. This is where the fashionistas congregate, hanging out in cafés and galleries, and mingling on the sidewalks. Barely a headscarf is visible. The streets looked nothing like this a few years ago, but once the American-Israeli attacks began in February this year, the Islamic Republic has been fighting for its survival: with much of its leadership killed, the Strait of Hormuz under siege, and many of the country’s neighbours in league with the enemy, policing what people wear has slipped a long way down its list of priorities.

The hijab law has been codified in Iran since 1983, enforced nationwide by the ‘morality’ police. Disobeying it meant fines, flogging or imprisonment. But then one act of disobedience changed everything. In December 2017, Vida Movahed, a woman in her 30s, climbed onto a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf and held it up on a stick. Although she was arrested and later sentenced to a year in prison, her action proved contagious. Other women climbed up onto boxes and makeshift plinths in the same street, waving their headscarves in the air. People began calling them the Girls of Enghelab Street. They were arrested too. It is hard to convey now how much nerve their actions took. Women had been edging their scarves back for years, but taking one off in daylight, above the traffic, where the police could see their naked heads as clearly as everyone else, was something very few women had done in public, since the protests of 1979 and 1980.

Then, in September 2022, Mahsa Jina Amini died in custody of the morality police. Unlike the women on the boxes, she was not an activist: aged 22, a Kurdish woman visiting from Saqqez, a city 600 km west of Tehran, she’d been stopped because her loose headscarf was not covering enough of her hair. Her death brought thousands of people out on to the street in an outpouring of grief and anger. Women burned their headscarves. Cut their hair in front of cameras. Their protests spawned the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, and continued for months. What began as a demand for justice for one woman became a challenge to the compulsory hijab, then to the system itself. The authorities responded with arrests, executions and a repression that has never really stopped. The funerals of the dead became protests in their turn.

W hat changed was that the morality police largely disappeared from the streets for months afterwards, with no announcement that the patrols had ended. Women who had grown up expecting to be stopped were not being stopped, and they knew why: the government had learned in 2022 what a single arrest could cost.

Azadeh, a woman from Tehran, tells me that, during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, the city felt apocalyptic. After the US president Donald Trump posted that people in Tehran should get out of the city, they fled their homes, leaving everything behind, and the city emptied. Checkpoints multiplied as the government waited for an uprising that never came. But in the strange mood that settled on the city following the attacks, Azadeh noticed another change – a bargain that nobody signed: ‘The state began leaving people alone to live as they like, as long as they do not come out into the street about it.’

‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together’

What is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of visible hair used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and New York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

Sima, also from Tehran, says that: ‘Among the women who dress freely there is a kind of solidarity. Nobody talks about it, but everyone feels it.’ Recalling the first time she removed her headscarf, Sima says: ‘I felt bald … I thought everyone was looking at me, and I kept checking.’ She was frightened, she told me, so she kept a headscarf in her bag ready to whip out if anything should happen. It took a while for the feeling to pass. Each time she went out, she saw more women without headscarves and that gave her heart. She knew that she was not alone.

T he easy read on these developments, especially outside Iran, is that this is defiance: using clothing as a weapon against the state. The framing is not entirely wrong, but it misses most of what is happening on the street, and the people living it do not describe what they are up to in this way. When I asked Mina if getting dressed felt like a political act, she paused, then said no. ‘When I dress up, it’s only for myself,’ she told me. ‘I’m not doing some political act.’ So what is happening on Iranshahr?

The Iranian sociologist Asef Bayat has spent years asking how ordinary people can change their societies in the absence of formal organisations or conventional political movements. In Life as Politics: How Ordinary People Change the Middle East (2010), he argues that they do it less by protesting than by simply living as they wish to, and in enough numbers and for long enough that the rules have to bend around them. Bayat’s name for what Sima, Mina and Azadeh are describing is ‘the art of presence’. It denotes ‘the courage and creativity to assert collective will in spite of all odds, to circumvent constraints, utilising what is available and discovering new spaces within which to make oneself heard, seen, felt, and realised.’ It is a form of soft power.
